system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-05-27 17:23:00 to 2170-06-05 12:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic idiopathic pancreatitis was admitted for a moderate flare characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, IV pain control including a Dilaudid PCA, and antiemetics. Due to slow improvement and moderate malnutrition, TPN was restarted and advanced to goal. Blood cultures, chest X-ray, and urinalysis showed no infection, and fevers resolved spontaneously. Her pain gradually improved to baseline, and she transitioned to oral hydromorphone while her fentanyl patch was reduced to 100 mcg/hr. She was advanced to a soft diet, managed for constipation, and continued on omeprazole twice daily for worsening GERD, with plans for outpatient EGD. She remained mentally clear, afebrile, and ambulatory, and was discharged home with TPN support, home health, and follow-up arranged.

You tolerated only pills for the day and a half prior to

We have spoken to the ___ care agency, ___, and they will

radiology_notes.text:
MRCP

INDICATION:  ___ woman with recent prolonged admission and recurrent
abdominal pain.  Currently on TPN due to recurrent pancreatitis.

Comparison was performed with previous MRCP study from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on 1.5 Tesla
magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior, during and after
uneventful intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg (15 cc) of
gadolinium-DTPA.  

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reconstructions and subtraction images were essential in
demonstrating the below findings.

FINDINGS:  The liver demonstrates normal signal intensity, apart from the
single lesion in segment VI of the liver, which demonstrates high-signal
intensity on T2-weighted images, with nearly homogeneous arterial and
portovenous enhancement, findings consistent with hemangioma.  There is no
evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.  Status post
cholecystectomy.

Pancreas demonstrates mild atrophy with normal signal intensity in the body
and tail of the pancreas, but decreased signal intensity of the parenchyma in
the head and uncinate process.  Further noted irregularity of the main
pancreatic duct with a number of dilated side branches in the body and tail of
pancreas (series 5, image 21 and series 7, image 1).

Adrenals are unremarkable bilaterally.  Kidneys are within normal limits apart
from a single simple cortical cyst in the upper pole of the right kidney. 
Spleen is within normal limits.  There is no evidence of retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  Visualized bowel loops are unremarkable.  Bone
marrow signal is within normal limits.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reconstructions and subtraction images were essential in
demonstrating the above findings.


IMPRESSION:
1.  Slight decreased signal intensity in the head and uncinate process of the
pancreas, which may correspond to chronic pancreatitis.

2.  Irregular contour of the non-dilated main pancreatic duct, more prominent
in the head and neck of the pancreas, along with mildly dilated side branches
in the body and tail of pancreas, unchanged from prior study, consistent with
chronic pancreatitis.

3.  No evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.

4.  Unchanged hemangioma in the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. You’re here because of severe abdominal pain again, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same kind of pain I’ve had before—right in the middle, going to my back. It didn’t get better with my usual pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged a day ago, but the pain came back quickly. We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth except meds—for now to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food or even sips of water? That’s tough, but I understand. My last stay was like that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you IV fluids and restart your TPN—total parenteral nutrition—so your body still gets what it needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been on TPN before. Will I go home on it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we plan to send you home on TPN again. Your GI doctor, Dr. Patel, is aware and will follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I just hope this flare doesn’t last as long as the last one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your labs. Your lipase was elevated at 666, which confirms pancreatitis, but your liver enzymes and kidney function are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there an infection? Last time I had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fevers this time, and your white blood cell count is normal. No signs of infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My mom had pancreatic cancer—do I need to worry about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. Your imaging doesn’t show anything suspicious. The changes are consistent with chronic pancreatitis, not cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We started your TPN yesterday. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less sharp. I’m on the fentanyl patch and hydromorphone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re giving IV anti-nausea meds too. We’ll keep you on IV pain control for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Is that from the narcotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re continuing your home bowel regimen—senna, docusate, and bisacodyl—and adding a few extra doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take those. I don’t want to feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRCP yesterday. It shows changes consistent with chronic pancreatitis—mild atrophy, irregular ducts—but no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a blockage or stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage or stones. The duct changes are stable compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver spot? Last time they said hemangioma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the liver hemangioma is still there, unchanged. It’s benign and not a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving. We’re going to try letting you take your pain meds by mouth today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have anything to drink with the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just small sips for now. We want to make sure you can tolerate oral meds before considering any diet changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll stick to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on oral pain meds. No need for IV doses since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to keep you NPO except for pills for a few more days. Your pancreas needs full rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s hard, but I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show stable hemoglobin at 10.0, which is your baseline. No anemia worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, but also from the illness and fasting. Once you’re home and on TPN, your energy should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. I miss being active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in two days if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need new prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re not changing your meds. You’ll go home on the same regimen, including the fentanyl patch and omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking hydromorphone every 3 hours at home. Can I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted that. You can take it every 3 to 4 hours as needed. We’ll make sure your prescription allows that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel it wears off by the fourth hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. No pain meds needed IV for over 24 hours. We’ll confirm discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will home health restart my TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the home care agency will restart it tonight. You have the nurse’s number to call with any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel safer knowing help is there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up an appointment with a pain clinic to review your opioid use and see if there are better options long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on these meds for years. I’d like to see if there’s a way to manage with less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great goal. The pain clinic can help with that safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your abdomen is now only minimally tender, and vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay NPO except for pills. Continue TPN as before. Take your meds as prescribed, especially for nausea and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my omeprazole? I take 40 mg twice a day at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, go back to your regular dose. We held it at 40 mg total in the hospital, but now you can resume your full regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my fentanyl patch—still two patches every 72 hours?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ve reduced it to one 100 mcg/hr patch every 72 hours, same as last discharge. It’s safer and still effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. Patel soon. Call us if pain worsens, or if you develop fever, vomiting, or trouble with TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in the clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my son has a CF gene mutation. Should I be tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s worth discussing with your PCP. It may be relevant given your chronic pancreatitis, but it’s not urgent now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll bring it up at my next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over discharge instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—should I avoid all movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you can walk and move normally. In fact, it’s good for you. Just avoid heavy lifting for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll stay active but careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s all we ask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for answering everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You can leave whenever you’re set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’ll get my things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic idiopathic pancreatitis was readmitted the day after discharge due to recurrent severe epigastric pain, nausea, and constipation unrelieved by oral medications. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and TPN restart. Pain was controlled with IV and transitioned to oral hydromorphone, with the fentanyl patch reduced to 100 mcg/hr. She tolerated oral medications for two days prior to discharge and required no IV medications in the final 24 hours. An MRCP showed stable chronic pancreatitis changes without new pathology. Constipation was managed with her home bowel regimen plus additional doses. She remained on her baseline psychiatric and GERD medications. No infectious source was found. She was discharged home with TPN, home health support, and follow-up arranged with her GI doctor and a new pain clinic consultation to address opioid dependence.
